config.prompt: Nine values — 2, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 15. Build the five-figure summary in order:
items: Sort the values — the sorted positions are the order statistics
Q1: median of the four below — (4+4)/2 = 4; Q3: median of the four above — (8+9)/2 = 8.5
IQR = 8.5 − 4 = 4.5 — the spread of the middle half
config.why: For grouped frequency tables the same quantities become interpolation estimates inside the containing class — the honest cost of grouped data.

activities.anchor: The three dispersion measures answer the same question
activities.caption: which summary earns which data?
activities.name: npDispSort

config.prompt: Outlier sensitivity decides the summary — file each case:

items.label: skewed incomes, and a billionaire joins the sample
clean, symmetric data where every point carries real information
instant, uses only two points, grows with sample size for pure sampling reasons
reaction times from a well-run laboratory experiment

config.why: A rank is a position — no value, however extreme, can be more extreme than 'largest'; the order statistics cap every observation's influence.

activities.caption: one line of this sign test is wrong — click it
activities.name: npSignSpot

config.prompt: One line of this sign-test write-up is wrong — click it:
lines: Paired data: keep only the direction of each change, + or −.
Eight patients, seven improved and one did not.
Under a fair-coin null: P(at least 7 of 8) = (C(8,7) + C(8,8))/2⁸ = 9/256.
Doubled for a two-tailed test: p ≈ 0.070 — conventionally significant at the 5% level.
The sign test throws away magnitudes entirely — its virtue is surviving ordinal scales.
config.correction: p ≈ 0.070 is suggestive but not conventionally significant — 0.070 is greater than 0.05.
config.why: The sign test's price is throwing magnitudes away; its payout is working where magnitudes are meaningless — 'better/worse' judgments, ratings.

activities.caption: fill in the tie's shared rank
activities.name: npTieCloze

config.text: When two values are equal they share the average of the ranks they span: two observations tied for 5th and 6th each take rank %%0%%. Heavy clusters of ties shrink the variance of U — and a 1-to-5 rating with thirty responses produces only %%1%% distinct values.
config.hint: Average the ranks they span; and count the possible ratings.

activities.anchor: upgrades the sign test for paired data
activities.caption: the family — pair each test with its brief
activities.name: npFamilyMatch

config.prompt: Match each rank method to the job it does:

pairs.right: paired data — ranks the absolute differences; assumes they are roughly symmetric
three or more independent groups — rank everything together, compare average ranks
correlates the ranks: ρ = 1 − 6Σd²/(n(n²−1)) for small samples without ties
ρ = 1 − 18/120 = 0.85 — the same 0.85 whether scores were 90 vs 91 or 90 vs 990

config.why: Only order enters the calculation — which is why rescaling the judges' scores leaves ρ untouched.

config.prompt: Under exact normality, Mann–Whitney's asymptotic relative efficiency against the t-test is about what value?
config.why: About 0.955 — a 4.5% sample-size penalty. Under heavy-tailed or contaminated data its efficiency exceeds the t-test's, unboundedly so for extreme tails.
config.context: The price of insurance is small and the payout is large exactly when you need it.

activities.anchor: The decision procedure is about the data
activities.caption: choose the analysis before the p-values exist
activities.name: npChoiceBranch

config.root: A pilot returns 18 ratings on a 1–5 scale, with a couple of extreme values. Choose the analysis.

start.text: Ordinal scale, small n, visible outliers. Which instrument?

choices.label: The t-test — the central limit theorem will save us
choices.feedback: The CLT drags the sampling distribution of the mean toward normality — but rescues tests of means slowly for heavy tails, and never rescues a single skew quantile.

choices.label: Mann–Whitney U on the ranks
choices.feedback: Rank methods cap every observation's influence — the right instrument for ordinal, outlier-prone data.

choices.label: A permutation test — shuffle the labels thousands of times
choices.feedback: No distributional assumption, exact in principle — Fisher imagined it in the 1930s; cheap computing delivered it.

clt.text: Forgiving with large samples, wobbling here — and the choice should have been made before the data.

ranks.text: A little power traded for a lot of robustness — an excellent trade with small, skewed data.

perm.text: Recompute the difference each shuffle and see where the real difference lands in the shuffle distribution.

config.why: Report both when in doubt: agreement is reassuring; disagreement is diagnostic — the conclusion hinges on a handful of extreme observations, and the write-up should say so.

activities.caption: true or false — the family's corners
activities.name: npCornerJudge

statements.s: Friedman handles several treatments measured on the same subjects — the taster as their own control.
statements.why: Rank the treatments within each subject, then ask whether the average ranks differ — the partner for taste panels and usability studies.

statements.s: Kruskal–Wallis is the tool for repeated measures on the same subjects.
statements.why: Kruskal–Wallis handles several independent groups; Friedman is the repeated-measures corner.

statements.s: The runs test asks whether a sequence is random — too few runs means clustering.
statements.why: Too few runs = streaks; too many = alternation — the tool for the 'hot hand' argument and for checking residuals.

statements.s: Too many runs in a binary series is the signature of streaks.
statements.why: Too many runs means alternation; streaks produce too few.
